subject: physics
title: Electric potential and comparing fields
key_idea: Electric potential at a point is the work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small test charge from infinity to the point. For a point charge V = Q/(4πε₀r). Field strength is minus the potential gradient, and electric and gravitational fields share many features.

blocks.text: Electric potential describes the energy per unit charge at a point in a field, measured from a zero at infinity.

items.meaning: The work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small test charge from infinity to the point.
The change in electric potential between two points.
A surface on which every point is at the same potential.

blocks.label: Potential of a point charge
where: ε₀ = permittivity of free space (8.85 × 10⁻¹² F/m)

items: Potential is **zero at infinity**.
V is positive near a positive charge and negative near a negative charge, so its sign matters.
V is a scalar and falls as 1/r, but the field E falls as 1/r².
The work done moving a charge Q through a potential difference ΔV is ΔW = QΔV.
No work is done moving a charge along an equipotential.
V is work done per unit positive charge from infinity, and V = Q/(4πε₀r).
V is a scalar, zero at infinity; its sign follows the sign of Q.
ΔW = QΔV, and no work is done along an equipotential.

blocks.text: Field strength and potential are linked: the field points in the direction in which the potential falls most steeply.

blocks.label: Field strength from the potential gradient

items: On a graph of V against r, the **gradient** at a point gives −E.
On a graph of E against r, the **area under the graph** between two distances is the change in potential ΔV.
On a graph of force against distance for a point or spherical charge, the area under the graph is the work done.
Between parallel plates the potential changes uniformly, so the gradient is constant and E = V/d.
Equipotentials are always at right angles to the field lines.
Around a point charge the equipotentials are **concentric spheres**, and they get further apart as r increases.
Between parallel plates the equipotentials are **equally spaced planes** parallel to the plates.
Field lines point from high to low potential.

blocks.label: Electric potential energy
blocks.formula: E_P = Q q / (4π ε₀ r) = q V
where: Q = the point charge producing the field (C)
q = the charge placed in the field (C)

items: Like charges: E_P is positive and increases as they are pushed closer.
Unlike charges: E_P is negative and becomes more negative as they come closer.
E_P is zero when the charges are infinitely far apart.

items: E = −ΔV/Δr; ΔV is the area under an E–r graph.
Equipotentials cross field lines at right angles.
E_P = Qq/(4πε₀r) = qV.

blocks.text: Electric and gravitational fields are two forms of field that give rise to a force. They have the same mathematical structure but differ in important ways.

diagram.alt: A comparison of the gravitational field of a point mass and the electric field of a point charge.
items: Gravitational field
Electric field

rows.feature: Field strength of a point source

items: Both have inverse-square force laws, so field strength and force fall as 1/r².
Both use field lines, potential and equipotential surfaces.
Both potentials are zero at infinity, and the potential falls as 1/r.
Gravity is always attractive, so gravitational potential is always negative; electric potential can be positive or negative.
Electric forces are far stronger than gravitational forces between particles.
Same form: inverse-square laws, field lines, potential and equipotentials.
Masses always attract; charges can attract or repel.
The constants are different: G for gravity, 1/(4πε₀) for electric fields.

checks.q: Define electric potential at a point.
checks.a: The work done per unit positive charge in bringing a small positive test charge from infinity to that point.

checks.q: A graph shows electric field strength E against distance r from a point charge. State how to find the potential difference between two distances.
checks.a: Find the area under the graph between the two values of r. This area equals the potential difference.

checks.q: State two similarities and two differences between the gravitational field of a point mass and the electric field of a point charge.
checks.a: Similarities: both obey an inverse-square law for force and field strength; both can be shown by field lines and equipotentials; both potentials fall as 1/r and are zero at infinity. Differences: gravity is always attractive but electric forces may attract or repel; gravitational field strength is force per unit mass but electric field strength is force per unit charge.

blocks.text: The electric field at a point equals the negative of the potential gradient at that point. Potential energy of two point charges follows from the potential.

items: Use E = −dV/dr, the negative of the gradient of the V–r graph.
E_P = Qq/(4πε₀r) follows because the potential energy of a charge q at potential V is qV.

blocks.text: Link electric fields with gravitational fields as two of several forms of field that give rise to a force.

items: Electric potential energy is Vq = Qq/(4πε₀r) at distance r from a point charge Q.
You may be asked to compare the field of a point mass with the field of a point charge.
